fetched_contents.text: Psychotic symptoms in bipolar disorder and their impact on the illness: A systematic review Abstract BACKGROUND Lifetime psychotic symptoms are present in over half of the patients with bipolar disorder (BD) and can have an adverse effect on its course, outcome, and treatment. However, despite a considerable amount of research, the impact of psychotic symptoms on BD remains unclear, and there are very few systematic reviews on the subject. AIM To examine the extent of psychotic symptoms in BD and their impact on several aspects of the illness. METHODS The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses guidelines were followed. An electronic literature search of six English-language databases and a manual search was undertaken to identify published articles on psychotic symptoms in BD from January 1940 to December 2021. Combinations of the relevant Medical Subject Headings terms were used to search for these studies. Articles were selected after a screening phase, followed by a review of the full texts of the articles. Assessment of the methodological quality of the studies and the risk of bias was conducted using standard tools. RESULTS This systematic review included 339 studies of patients with BD. Lifetime psychosis was found in more than a half to two-thirds of the patients, while current psychosis was found in a little less than half of them. Delusions were more common than hallucinations in all phases of BD. About a third of the patients reported first-rank symptoms or mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms, particularly during manic episodes. Psychotic symptoms were more frequent in bipolar type I compared to bipolar type II disorder and in mania or mixed episodes compared to bipolar depression. Although psychotic symptoms were not more severe in BD, the severity of the illness in psychotic BD was consistently greater. Methods Participants from the Suffolk County Mental Health Project (SCMHP) with a baseline diagnosis of bipolar I disorder with psychotic features (N = 126) were reassessed using face-to-face interviews at six months, two years, and four years following their first hospitalization. Branch 1: What the literature says about setting-specific prevalence

The literature indicates that psychotic symptoms are common in bipolar disorder overall, but the prevalence differs by setting. The highest-quality systematic review/meta-analysis reports that the pooled point prevalence of psychotic symptoms in bipolar disorder overall was 54% (95% CI 41–67), with 57% (95% CI 47–66) in manic episodes and 13% (95% CI 7–) in depressive episodes [N1-F1]. A separate source in the same set of results also notes that the pooled point prevalence in bipolar depression was 13% (95% CI 7–), while manic episodes had 57% (95% CI 47–66) [N1-R2]. Another source in the same evidence set says that lifetime rates of psychosis were about 40–60% in mania and mixed episodes but only about 20% in bipolar depression episodes [N1-R5]. This suggests that inpatient, outpatient, and depressive episode settings differ substantially: mania and mixed episodes are consistently associated with much higher prevalence than bipolar depression.

Across the evidence provided, the settings that report higher prevalence are manic episodes and mixed episodes, while depressive episodes report lower prevalence. The review also notes that current rates of psychosis are about three times higher in mania than in bipolar depression [N6-R1]. This is consistent with the broader literature that psychotic symptoms are much more frequent during manic than depressive episodes [N5-F3]. The evidence also includes an acute-episode study reporting that 52.7% of patients in the acute episode of bipolar disease had psychotic symptoms [N1-R4], which reinforces that acute episodes are associated with high prevalence. However, the evidence does not provide a direct outpatient prevalence estimate in the provided fragments, so that comparison must be inferred cautiously.

The literature also suggests that symptom measurement varies across studies, which affects comparisons. The review explicitly includes a large number of heterogeneous studies and reports that lifetime and point prevalence were extracted from 297 studies after full-text screening [N1-F1]. It also notes that assessment of study quality and risk of bias was conducted using standard tools [N1-F1]. This implies that different studies may use different operationalizations, duration of assessment, and thresholds for identifying psychotic symptoms. The evidence further indicates that diagnostic criteria and symptom thresholds are important context for interpretation, because one source notes that bipolar I disorder with psychotic features is common in inpatient settings and outcomes vary after hospital discharge [N5-F3]. Another source points to the role of mood-congruent versus mood-incongruent symptoms and first-rank symptoms, suggesting that studies may define psychosis differently depending on whether they focus on delusions, hallucinations, or more severe features [N4-F2]. In addition, the evidence from the systematic review indicates that psychotic symptoms may be more common in bipolar type I than type II and in mania or mixed episodes than bipolar depression [N4-F2]. This variation in operationalization can make direct comparisons across settings difficult unless the studies are comparable in criteria, severity thresholds, and episode definitions.

Overall, the literature supports the conclusion that setting-specific prevalence varies: manic/mixed episodes and acute episodes tend to report higher prevalence than depressive episodes, and outpatient studies may be harder to interpret because of differing symptom thresholds, episode definitions, and risk-of-bias factors [N1-F1][N4-F2][N5-F3]. The evidence is strongest for manic episodes and mixed episodes, weaker for outpatient-specific prevalence, and suggestive but less precise for bipolar depression alone [N1-R5][N1-R2][N1-R4].

Branch 3: Methodological and diagnostic factors that explain apparent differences

The apparent differences in prevalence across settings can be explained by study design, setting, and sample selection differences. The evidence shows that the systematic review/meta-analysis included 297 studies after full-text screening and 78 studies for meta-analysis, with different studies reporting lifetime and point prevalence [N1-F1]. It also notes that assessment of study quality and risk of bias was conducted using validated risk-of-bias tools appropriate to study design [N1-F1]. This implies that studies vary in design, and that differences in study quality may explain apparent differences in prevalence estimates.

Study design differences are evident in the evidence set. One source reports that bipolar disorder with psychosis is common in inpatient settings and that outcomes can range from return to premorbid functioning to chronic or recurring illness [N5-F3]. Another source notes that bipolar I disorder with psychosis is common in inpatient settings and that outcomes after hospital discharge are diverse [N5-F3]. In contrast, the evidence from the systematic review suggests that depressive episodes have lower prevalence estimates than manic episodes [N1-F1]. These differences may reflect the fact that inpatient settings are more likely to capture severe or acute presentations, while outpatient settings may include milder or less symptomatic cases [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The evidence also points to sample selection bias in some studies: one source explicitly states that a study used propensity scoring to control for selection bias and that it used retrospective, longitudinal claims data [N3-R1]. Another source notes that a study reduced selection bias and that recall bias was excluded, suggesting that some studies may be less prone to selection bias than others [N3-R5]. These design differences can explain why some studies report higher prevalence than others.

Diagnostic criteria and symptom thresholds also affect prevalence estimates. The evidence indicates that psychotic symptoms are defined broadly as either delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech, and that mood-congruent and mood-incongruent symptoms, as well as first-rank symptoms, occur in bipolar disorder [N2-R1][N4-F2]. Because of this broad definition, studies may capture different symptom severity profiles. The systematic review notes that lifetime psychosis was present in more than half of patients and that current psychosis was found in a little less than half of them [N4-F2]. It also reports that delusions were more common than hallucinations in all phases of BD and that about a third of patients reported first-rank symptoms or mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms, particularly during manic episodes [N4-F2]. This shows that symptom thresholds matter: studies using broader definitions may report higher prevalence than those using narrower, more severe thresholds. The same systematic review also notes that psychotic symptoms may be more frequent in bipolar type I than in type II disorder and in mania or mixed episodes than in bipolar depression [N4-F2]. This suggests that diagnostic criteria for bipolar subtype and episode type shape prevalence estimates.

Limitations and caveats for interpreting cross-setting comparisons are clear. The evidence shows that prevalence estimates come from heterogeneous study designs, including lifetime studies, point prevalence studies, and inpatient/outpatient cohorts [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Because of this heterogeneity, direct comparisons across settings are not straightforward. The systematic review explicitly reports that lifetime and point prevalence were extracted from different studies and that the meta-analysis included a large number of heterogeneous studies [N1-F1]. It also notes that assessment of methodological quality and risk of bias was conducted [N1-F1], indicating that some studies may be more reliable than others. The evidence further suggests that outpatient studies may be especially sensitive to selection bias, because one source explicitly addresses selection bias in a claims-data study and another notes that recall bias can be excluded in some designs [N3-R1][N3-R5]. In addition, the evidence indicates that acute-episode studies may capture more severe presentations, while outpatient studies may miss or underestimate psychosis if symptoms are mild or not formally assessed [N5-F3][N1-R4]. Overall, cross-setting comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because of differences in study design, setting, sample selection, diagnostic criteria, and symptom thresholds [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F2].

The evidence indicates that prevalence differs between acute episode and outpatient settings, with acute episodes generally associated with higher prevalence. One source reports that in an acute episode of bipolar disease, 52.7% of patients had psychotic symptoms, which the author describes as a high prevalence [N1-R4]. The same systematic review/meta-analysis reports that lifetime rates of psychosis were about 40–60% in mania and mixed episodes but only about 20% in bipolar depression episodes [N1-R5], and that current rates of psychosis were about three times higher in mania than in bipolar depression [N6-R1]. This suggests that acute episodes, especially manic or mixed acute episodes, are more likely to present with psychosis than outpatient settings.

Acute episode studies provide important information about severity and promptness of psychosis detection. The evidence shows that acute episodes are associated with higher prevalence and that psychosis in acute episodes may be more severe or more readily apparent. Another source notes that **lifetime rates of psychosis were about three times higher in mania than in bipolar depression**, and that **current rates of psychosis were about three times higher in mania than in bipolar depression** [N6-R1]. This suggests that acute manic or mixed episodes are more likely to present with psychosis than depressive episodes.

### b) Inpatient selection bias
Inpatient settings are more likely to capture severe or acute cases, which can increase prevalence. The evidence indicates that **bipolar I disorder with psychosis is common in inpatient settings** and that outcomes after hospital discharge vary widely [N5-F3]. Another source says that **bipolar I disorder with psychosis is the second most common diagnosis among inpatients admitted with prominent psychotic symptoms** [N5-F3]. This implies that inpatient studies may overrepresent psychosis because they include patients who are hospitalized for more severe or urgent presentations.

### c) Outpatient underascertainment
Outpatient studies may miss psychosis because they may include milder cases or cases that are not formally assessed as rigorously as inpatient studies. The branch reports note that prevalence estimates come from heterogeneous study designs and that **symptom measurement and operationalization vary across studies** [N1-F1][N4-F2]. They also suggest that outpatient studies may underestimate psychosis if symptoms are mild or not formally captured in routine care [N5-F3]. In contrast, outpatient studies may sometimes overestimate psychosis if they include patients with mild symptoms that are not captured in inpatient cohorts [N5-F3].

---

## 3) Episode type and mixed/mood-concurrent states

The branch reports show that **episode type strongly influences psychosis prevalence**, with manic episodes and mixed episodes having the highest rates and depressive episodes having the lowest.

### a) Prevalence across episode types
The evidence reports that **lifetime rates of psychosis were about 40–60% in mania and mixed episodes but only about 20% in bipolar depression episodes** [N1-R5]. It also notes that **current rates of psychosis were about three times higher in mania than in bipolar depression** [N6-R1]. Another source says that **psychotic symptoms were more frequent in bipolar type I than in bipolar type II disorder and in mania or mixed episodes compared to bipolar depression** [N4-F2]. These findings support a clear hierarchy: **mixed episodes and manic episodes have the highest prevalence, while bipolar depression has the lowest**.

### b) Mood-concurrent versus depressive psychosis
The evidence indicates that **mood-congruent and mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms, as well as first-rank symptoms, occur in bipolar disorder** [N2-R1][N4-F2]. It also reports that **about a third of patients reported first-rank symptoms or mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms, particularly during manic episodes** [N4-F2]. This suggests that **mood-concurrent psychosis is common and easier to recognize**, especially in manic episodes, while **depressive psychosis may be less prominent but still clinically meaningful**.

### c) Clinical features and outcomes in depressive states
Even when psychosis occurs in depressive states, the evidence suggests that it is associated with adverse outcomes. One source reports that **psychotic symptoms during episodes in patients with BD are associated with poorer course of BD** [N4-R2]. Another source notes that **psychotic symptoms were not more severe in BD, but the severity of the illness in psychotic BD was consistently greater** [N4-F2]. It also reports that psychosis was associated with **poor insight, higher frequency of agitation, anxiety, and hostility**, and with **increased rates and duration of hospitalizations, switching among patients with depression, and poorer outcomes with mood-incongruent symptoms** [N4-F2]. In contrast, psychosis was less likely to be accompanied by a rapid-cycling course, longer illness duration, and heightened suicidal risk [N4-F2].

The evidence also shows that **psychosis during bipolar depressive episodes can occur in outpatient samples** and that **psychotic, depressed patients had worse outcomes** [N5-R4]. This indicates that even in less severe depressive states, psychosis can still have negative consequences.

---

## 4) Methodological and diagnostic factors that explain apparent differences

The branch reports emphasize that differences in prevalence across settings are not always due to true differences in disease biology, but rather to differences in **study design, setting, sample selection, diagnostic criteria, and symptom thresholds** [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F2].

### a) Study design and setting differences
The evidence shows that studies differ by setting: **inpatient studies** are more likely to capture severe or acute psychosis, while **outpatient studies** may include milder or less formally assessed cases [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The systematic review/meta-analysis explicitly reports that **lifetime and point prevalence were extracted from 297 studies after full-text screening** and that **assessment of study quality and risk of bias was conducted using standard tools** [N1-F1]. This heterogeneity makes direct comparisons difficult.

### b) Sample selection bias
Some studies use retrospective, longitudinal claims data and control for selection bias [N3-R1]. Another source notes that **selection bias is reduced in our study and recall bias is excluded** [N3-R5]. These design differences can explain why some studies report higher prevalence than others.

### c) Diagnostic criteria and symptom thresholds
The evidence indicates that psychotic symptoms are defined broadly as **delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech** [N2-R1]. Mood-congruent and mood-incongruent symptoms, as well as first-rank symptoms, also occur in bipolar disorder [N4-F2]. Because of this broad definition, studies may capture different symptom severity profiles. The systematic review reports that **delusions were more common than hallucinations in all phases of BD** and that **about a third of patients reported first-rank symptoms or mood-incongruent psychotic symptoms, particularly during manic episodes** [N4-F2]. This suggests that symptom thresholds matter: broader definitions can increase prevalence estimates.

### d) Limitations for cross-setting comparisons
The branch reports caution that cross-setting comparisons should be interpreted cautiously because of **heterogeneous study designs, different episode definitions, and varying symptom thresholds** [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F2]. They also note that outpatient studies may miss psychosis and that acute episode studies may overrepresent severe cases [N5-F3]. As a result, apparent differences in prevalence may reflect study design rather than true biological differences.

---

## 5) Acute episode vs outpatient evidence and implications

The branch reports indicate that **acute episode settings report higher prevalence of psychotic symptoms than outpatient settings**, especially for manic and mixed episodes [N1-R4][N1-R5][N6-R1]. Acute episode studies are useful for detecting severe psychosis and for understanding **severity and promptness of psychosis detection** [N5-F3][N4-F2].

### a) Severity and promptness of psychosis detection
Acute episodes are associated with higher prevalence because psychosis is more severe and more likely to prompt hospitalization. One source notes that **bipolar I disorder with psychosis is common in inpatient settings** and that outcomes after hospital discharge vary widely [N5-F3]. Another source reports that patients hospitalized for bipolar I disorder with psychosis were reassessed at six months, two years, and four years following their first hospitalization, with **a large majority returning to premorbid functioning** but **almost half being rehospitalized at least once** [N5-F3]. This suggests that acute psychosis is often severe enough to prompt hospitalization, but that the illness course after discharge can still be favorable in many cases.

### b) Outpatient studies may miss or overestimate psychosis
Outpatient studies may miss psychosis because they may not capture severe or acute presentations and because symptom measurement varies across studies [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that outpatient studies may overestimate psychosis if they include patients with mild symptoms that are not formally assessed in inpatient settings [N5-F3]. At the same time, outpatient studies may still detect psychosis, as shown by the evidence that **psychosis during bipolar depressive episodes was present even in an outpatient sample** [N5-R4]. This shows that psychosis can occur in outpatient settings, but its detection may be incomplete.

---

## 6) Bottom line

Putting the evidence together, the prevalence of psychotic symptoms in bipolar disorder differs across inpatient, outpatient, and depressive episode settings in a predictable way:

- **Manic/mixed episodes** have the **highest prevalence**, with lifetime rates about 40–60% and current rates up to three times higher than in depressive episodes [N1-R5][N6-R1].
- **Depressive episodes** have the **lowest prevalence**, with current rates about 13% and lifetime rates about 20% [N1-R5].
- **Inpatient settings** are likely to report higher prevalence because they capture severe or acute presentations [N5-F3].
- **Outpatient settings** may miss psychosis due to milder cases or less rigorous assessment, but they can still detect it, especially in depressive states [N5-F3][N5-R4].
- **Acute episodes** tend to report higher prevalence than outpatient settings, especially for manic and mixed episodes [N1-R4][N1-R5][N6-R1].

The branch reports also caution that these differences should be interpreted cautiously because of **study design, setting, sample selection, diagnostic criteria, and symptom thresholds** [N1-F1][N3-R1][N3-R5][N4-F2]. The evidence supports the conclusion that **psychotic symptoms are common in bipolar disorder overall, but they are unevenly distributed across settings and episode types**.
